CC.description:
DIV{HEADER1{CC,  -- the class of all complex numbers}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, In Macaulay2, complex numbers are represented as floating point numbers, and so are only approximate.  The symbol , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ii},  represents the square root of -1 in many numeric contexts.  A complex number is obtained by using the symbolic constant , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ii},  or the conversion functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toCC},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: numeric}, , in combination with real numbers (see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RR}, ). It is stored internally as a pair of arbitrary precision floating point real numbers, using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFR},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : z = 3-4*ii

o1 = 3-4*ii

o1 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : z^5

o2 = -237.0000000000017+3115.999999999999*ii

o2 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : 1/z

o3 = .12+.16*ii

o3 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : +ii

o4 = ii

o4 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : numeric_200 ii

o5 = ii

o5 : CC (of precision 200), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Complex numbers are ordered lexicographically, mingled with real numbers., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : sort {1+ii,2+ii,1-ii,2-ii,1/2,2.1,7/5}

      1              7
o6 = {-, 1-ii, 1+ii, -, 2-ii, 2+ii, 2.1}
      2              5

o6 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : precision z

o7 = 53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, For complex numbers, the functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: class},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ring},  yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : class z

o8 = CC

o8 : InexactFieldFamily, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : ring z

o9 = CC
       53

o9 : ComplexField, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, A computation involving numbers of different precisions has a result with the minimal precision occurring. Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.), TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : 3p100+2p90e3*ii

o10 = 3+2000*ii

o10 : CC (of precision 90), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers displayed inside more complicated objects are printed with the number of digits specified by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: printingPrecision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : printingPrecision

o11 = 6, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : x = {1/3.*ii,1/3p100*ii}

o12 = {.333333*ii, .333333*ii}

o12 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Use , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toExternalString},  to produce something that, when encountered as input, will reproduce exactly what you had before., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : y = toExternalString x

o13 = {toCC(.0p53,.33333333333333331p53),toCC(.0p100
      ,.33333333333333333333333333333346p100)}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i14 : value y === x

o14 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Caveat}, Currently, most transcendental functions are not implemented for complex arguments.}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc RR.description:
DIV{HEADER1{RR,  -- the class of all real numbers}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A real number is entered as a sequence of decimal digits with a point.  It is stored internally as an arbitrary precision floating point number, using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFR},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : 3.14159

o1 = 3.14159

o1 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : precision 3.14159

o2 = 53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, For real numbers, the functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: class},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ring},  yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : class 3.1

o3 = RR

o3 : InexactFieldFamily, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : ring 3.1

o4 = RR
       53

o4 : RealField, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision can be specified on input by appending the letter , TT{p},  and a positive number., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : 3p300

o5 = 3

o5 : RR (of precision 300), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, An optional exponent (for the power of ten to multiply by) can be specified on input by appending the letter , TT{e},  and a number., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : 3e3

o6 = 3000

o6 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : -3e-3

o7 = -.003

o7 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : -3p111e-3

o8 = -.003

o8 : RR (of precision 111), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.), TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : 1/3.

o9 = .3333333333333333

o9 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : 1/3p100

o10 = .3333333333333333333333333333335

o10 : RR (of precision 100), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : 100 * log(10,2)

o11 = 30.10299956639811

o11 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers displayed inside more complicated objects are printed with the number of digits specified by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: printingPrecision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : printingPrecision

o12 = 6, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : {1/3.,1/3p100}

o13 = {.333333, .333333}

o13 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ==},  amounts to equality of the internal binary digits., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i14 : .5p100 == .5p30

o14 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i15 : .2p100 == .2p30

o15 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of (strict) equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ===},  also takes the precision into account., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i16 : .5p100 === .5p30

o16 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i17 : .2p100 === .2p30

o17 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Perhaps surprisingly, the IEEE floating point standard also specifies that every number, including 0, has a sign bit, and strict equality testing takes it into account, as it must do, because some arithmetic and transcendental functions take it into account., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i18 : 0.

o18 = 0

o18 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i19 : -0.

o19 = -0

o19 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i20 : 1/0.

o20 = infinity

o20 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i21 : 1/-0.

o21 = -infinity

o21 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i22 : log 0

o22 = -infinity

o22 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i23 : csc (0.)

o23 = infinity

o23 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i24 : csc (-0.)

o24 = -infinity

o24 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Use , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toExternalString},  to produce something that, when encountered as input, will reproduce exactly what you had before., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i25 : x = {1/3.,1/3p100}

DIV{HEADER1{addCone,  -- adds cones to a Fan}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{F1 = addCone(C,F) , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{F1 = addCone(L,F), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{C}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Cone, convex rational cone}}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{L}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}, , , with elements of class , TO{Polyhedra :: Cone},  or , TO{Polyhedra :: Fan}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{F}, , , SPAN{an instance of the type , TO{Polyhedra :: Fan}}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{F1}, , , SPAN{an instance of the type , TO{Polyhedra :: Fan}}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{}, If , TT{addCone},  is applied to a , TO{Polyhedra :: Cone},  and a , TO{Polyhedra :: Fan},  it adds the Cone to the Fan if they are in the same ambient space, if the Cone is compatible with every generating Cone of , TT{F}, , but is not a face of one of them. If one of the first two conditions fails, there will be an error and no fan will be returned. The pairs of incompatible cones can be accessed with the function , TO{Polyhedra :: incompCones}, . If the last condition fails, then the cone is already in the fan as a face of one of the cones, so it does not have to be added. The conditions are checked in this order., PARA{}, If , TT{addCone},  is applied to a , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: List},  and a , TO{Polyhedra :: Fan}, , then the function adds the list cone by cone and stops if one of the three conditions fails for one of the cones. There is again an error for the first two conditions. The pairs of incompatible cones can again be retrieved using , TO{Polyhedra :: incompCones}, ., PARA{}, If applied to a pair of fans it adds the generating cones of the first fan to the second fan, again checking for the same conditions as above., PARA{},  As an example, we make a fan consisting of the following cone and try to add an adjacent orthant., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : C = coneFromVData matrix {{1,0,0},{0,1,1},{0,0,1}};, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : F = fan C

o2 = F

o2 : Fan, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : C = coneFromVData matrix {{-1,0,0},{0,1,0},{0,0,1}};, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : incompCones(C,F)

o4 = {(C, Cone{...1...})}

o4 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, This shows that the two cones do not intersect in a common face, but if we divide C into two parts, we get a fan., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : C1 = intersection {C, coneFromHData(matrix {{0,1,-1}})};, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : C2 = intersection {C, coneFromHData(matrix {{0,-1,1}})};, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : F = addCone({C1,C2},F)

o7 = F

o7 : Fan, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{addCone}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{addCone(Cone,Fan)}}, LI{KBD{addCone(List,Fan)}}, LI{TOH{Polyhedra :: addCone(Fan,Cone)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Polyhedra :: addCone},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Polyhedra/documentation/old_documentation.m2:681:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{antipode,  -- antipode for skew commuting polynomial rings}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{antipode f, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{f}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingElement, ring element}}, , , TEX{An element in any ring}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingElement, ring element}}, , , TEX{An element in the same ring, the antipode of f}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If the ring does not have skew commuting variables, antipode is the identify function.}}, PARA{TEX{If the ring does have skew commuting variables, then the antipode returns a new polynomial with the same monomials, and the coefficients have been modified to provide an isomorphism with the ring, and its opposite ring, i.e. this switches left and right modules of the ring.}}, PARA{TEX{This is implemented in the following simple manner: each monomial which has exactly $d$ skew commuting variables occurring (thus, with exponent 1 each), is multiplied by $(-1)^{(d-1)(d-2)/2}$.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = ZZ/32003[a..f, SkewCommutative => true]

o1 = R

o1 : PolynomialRing, 6 skew commutative variable(s), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : F = 1 + a + b + a*b + b*c*d + a*b*c*d*e

o2 = a*b*c*d*e + b*c*d + a*b + a + b + 1

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : antipode F

o3 = a*b*c*d*e - b*c*d - a*b + a + b + 1

o3 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If the ring has some skew commuting variables, and some commutative ones, then only the skew ones are considered.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : S = ZZ/32003[a..f, SkewCommutative => {0,1,2}]

o4 = S

o4 : PolynomialRing, 3 skew commutative variable(s), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : F = 1 + a + b + a*b + b*c*d + a*b*c*d*e

o5 = a*b*c*d*e + b*c*d + a*b + a + b + 1

o5 : S, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : antipode F

o6 = - a*b*c*d*e - b*c*d - a*b + a + b + 1

o6 : S, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The transpose of a matrix applies this function to each entry.  This is basically because the transpose of a left module gives a right module, and we need to make that a left module again.  The key reason for this is so that the transpose of a complex remains a complex.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : use R

o7 = R

o7 : PolynomialRing, 6 skew commutative variable(s), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : M = matrix{{a*b-1, a*c-d, e-a*b*c}}

o8 = | ab-1 ac-d -abc+e |

             1      3
o8 : Matrix R  <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : N = syz M

o9 = {2} | -ad 0  cd   be ae -abd+ac-d -abc-bd -bcd 2abd-ac+d abc-abe-e
     {2} | a   cd bd-c 0  0  1         b       bc   -ab-1     0        
     {3} | 0   0  0    b  a  0         0       0    0         -1       
     ------------------------------------------------------------------------
     bde+ce abce |
     be     0    |
     c      e    |

             3      12
o9 : Matrix R  <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : M*N

o10 = 0

              1      12
o10 : Matrix R  <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : (transpose N) * (transpose M)

o11 = 0

              12      1
o11 : Matrix R   <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If we had not used the antipode, then this would be false!}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : Mt = matrix transpose entries M -- this does not use antipode

o12 = | ab-1   |
      | ac-d   |
      | -abc+e |

              3      1
o12 : Matrix R  <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : Nt = matrix transpose entries N -- this does not use antipode

o13 = | -ad       a     0  |
      | 0         cd    0  |
      | cd        bd-c  0  |
      | be        0     b  |
      | ae        0     a  |
      | -abd+ac-d 1     0  |
      | -abc-bd   b     0  |
      | -bcd      bc    0  |
      | 2abd-ac+d -ab-1 0  |
      | abc-abe-e 0     -1 |
      | bde+ce    be    c  |
      | abce      0     e  |

              12      3
o13 : Matrix R   <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i14 : Nt*Mt -- is not zero!

o14 = | 2ad    |
      | 0      |
      | -2cd   |
      | -2be   |
      | -2ae   |
      | 0      |
      | 2bd    |
      | 0      |
      | 0      |
      | 0      |
      | -2ce   |
      | -2abce |

              12      1
o14 : Matrix R   <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Caveat}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If the ring is a Weyl algebra, the antipode is the identity, which is probably not what is wanted.  If the ring is a quotient of a skew commuting polynomial ring $R/I$, then the antipode of an element should really be in the quotient ring $R/(antipode(I))$, but this function returns an element in the same ring.}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: transpose}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{antipode}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{antipode(RingElement)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: antipode},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/antipode-doc.m2:62:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{barycentricTriangulation,  -- computes a triangulation of a polytope}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{L = barycentricTriangulation P, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{P}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron, convex polyhedron}}, , , , which must be compact}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{L}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}, , ,  containing the simplices of the triangulation}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{}, TT{barycentricTriangulation},   computes the triangulation of the polyhedron , TT{P}, , if it is compact, i.e. a polytope, recursively. CC.description:
DIV{HEADER1{CC,  -- the class of all complex numbers}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, In Macaulay2, complex numbers are represented as floating point numbers, and so are only approximate.  The symbol , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ii},  represents the square root of -1 in many numeric contexts.  A complex number is obtained by using the symbolic constant , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ii},  or the conversion functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toCC},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: numeric}, , in combination with real numbers (see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RR}, ). It is stored internally as a pair of arbitrary precision floating point real numbers, using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFR},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : z = 3-4*ii

o1 = 3-4*ii

o1 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : z^5

o2 = -237.0000000000017+3115.999999999999*ii

o2 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : 1/z

o3 = .12+.16*ii

o3 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : +ii

o4 = ii

o4 : CC (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : numeric_200 ii

o5 = ii

o5 : CC (of precision 200), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Complex numbers are ordered lexicographically, mingled with real numbers., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : sort {1+ii,2+ii,1-ii,2-ii,1/2,2.1,7/5}

      1              7
o6 = {-, 1-ii, 1+ii, -, 2-ii, 2+ii, 2.1}
      2              5

o6 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : precision z

o7 = 53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, For complex numbers, the functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: class},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ring},  yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : class z

o8 = CC

o8 : InexactFieldFamily, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : ring z

o9 = CC
       53

o9 : ComplexField, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, A computation involving numbers of different precisions has a result with the minimal precision occurring. Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.), TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : 3p100+2p90e3*ii

o10 = 3+2000*ii

o10 : CC (of precision 90), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers displayed inside more complicated objects are printed with the number of digits specified by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: printingPrecision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : printingPrecision

o11 = 6, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : x = {1/3.*ii,1/3p100*ii}

o12 = {.333333*ii, .333333*ii}

o12 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Use , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toExternalString},  to produce something that, when encountered as input, will reproduce exactly what you had before., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : y = toExternalString x

o13 = {toCC(.0p53,.33333333333333331p53),toCC(.0p100

Classic.description:
DIV{HEADER1{Classic,  -- a parser for classic Macaulay syntax}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{This package provides a parser for polynomials in the classic Macaulay format.  Some users prefer it, for ease and speed of typing polynomials, ideals, and matrices.}, PARA{Only ring variables that are single letters, or single letters indexed by a sequence of numbers can be handled with this parser.}, PARA{The rules for creating polynomials using the classic parser include:}, UL{LI{Spaces, tabs, and newline characters are completely ignored.}, LI{A variable is either (1) a single letter, (2) a subscripted variable, or (3) a polynomial enclosed in parentheses.}, LI{Subscripted variables, e.g., , TT{y_(1,1)}, , are written using brackets, as in , TT{y[1,1]}, . Instead of explicit numbers for subscripted variables, Macaulay2 user variables that have an integer value may be used.}, LI{Coefficients are either integers or rational numbers, starting with a + or - (which may be omitted for the first monomial).  Over finite fields, the division is performed in that field.}, LI{A monomial is written without symbols for multiplication or exponentiation, where the (optional) coefficient comes first.}, LI{A polynomial is a collection of monomials one after the other.}, LI{Parenthesized subexpressions are allowed.}, LI{Except for indices for subscripted variables, integers must be explicitly given.}, LI{All of the variables used must already belong to a specific ring.  If in doubt, first type , TT{use R},  to ensure that all the symbols of , TT{R},  are in use.}}, PARA{The source code for this parser is relatively short, since it is based on the package , TO{Parsing :: Parsing}, .  Here it is.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{export "poly"
symbolP = (x -> (
          if not isGlobalSymbol x then error("symbol ",x," undefined");
          getGlobalSymbol x)) % letterParser
seqP = (comma, parser) -> prepend % parser @ * (last % comma @ parser)
variableP = value % symbolP
intP = NNParser | variableP
subscriptP = ((lb,x,rb) -> x) % andP( "[", unsequence % seqP_"," intP, "]" )
ringVariableP = ((x,n) -> value if n === nil then x else x_n) % 
                symbolP @ optP subscriptP
numberP = ZZParser | QQParser
powerP = ((x,n) -> if n === nil then x else x^n) % 
         (futureParser parenExprP | ringVariableP) @ optP NNParser
monomialP = times @@ deepSplice % 
            optionalSignParser @ (numberP @ *powerP | +powerP )
polyP = plus @@ deepSplice % +monomialP | terminalParser 0
parenExprP = ((l,x,r) -> x) % andP("(", futureParser parenExprP | polyP, ")")
listPolyP = toList % seqP_"," polyP
arrayPolyP = toList % seqP_";" listPolyP
poly = method()
polyParser = polyP : nonspaceAnalyzer
poly String :=  RingElement => x -> polyParser x
idealParser = ideal % listPolyP : nonspaceAnalyzer
ideal String := Ideal => x -> idealParser x
monomialIdealParser = monomialIdeal % listPolyP : nonspaceAnalyzer
monomialIdeal String := MonomialIdeal => x -> monomialIdealParser x
matrix String := Matrix => 
                 opts -> matrix_opts % arrayPolyP : nonspaceAnalyzer}}}}}, MENU{TO{Classic :: poly(String)}, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ideal(String)}, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: matrix(String)}}, DIV{DIV{DIV{HEADER2{Author}, UL{LI{HREF{http://www.math.uiuc.edu/~dan/, Daniel R. Grayson}, SPAN{ <, HREF{mailto:dan@math.uiuc.edu, dan@math.uiuc.edu}, >}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Version}, PARA{This documentation describes version , BOLD{1.0},  of , Classic, , released , BOLD{June, 2006}, .}}, DIV{HEADER2{Citation}, PARA{If you have used , this package,  in your research, please cite it as follows:}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{class => language-bib, @misc{ClassicSource,
  title = {{Classic: a classic Macaulay parser. Version~1.0}},
  author = {Daniel R. Grayson},
  howpublished = {A \emph{Macaulay2} package available at
    \url{https://github.com/Macaulay2/M2/tree/stable/M2/Macaulay2/packages}}
}
}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Exports}, DIV{class => exports, UL{LI{Functions and commands, UL{LI{SPAN{KBD{poly},  -- see , TOH{Classic :: poly(String)}}}}}, LI{Methods, UL{LI{TOH{Classic :: ideal(String)}}, LI{TOH{Classic :: matrix(String)}}, LI{TOH{Classic :: monomialIdeal(String)}}, LI{TOH{Classic :: poly(String)}}}}}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Classic :: Classic},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Package, package}}, , defined in , TT{Classic.m2}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Classic.m2:85:0}, .}}}}

combine.description:
DIV{HEADER1{combine,  -- combine hash tables}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{z = combine(x,y,f,g,h) or z=combine(x,y,f,t,g,h), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{x}, , , a hash table}}, LI{SPAN{TT{y}, , , a hash table of the same class as , TT{x}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{f}, , , a function of two variables to be used for combining a key of , TT{x},  with a key of , TT{y},  to make a new key for , TT{z}, .}}, LI{SPAN{TT{t}, , , a function combining two keys and returning a value, twisting the value returned by , TT{g},  based on which keys were used. This argument may be omitted, in which case the , TT{t(p,q)},  term in the output below is omitted.}}, LI{SPAN{TT{g}, , , a function of two variables to be used for combining a value of , TT{x},  with a value of , TT{y},  to make a new value for , TT{z}, .}}, LI{SPAN{TT{h}, , , a function of two variables to be used for combining two values returned by , TT{g},  when the corresponding keys returned by , TT{f},  turn out to be equal.  Its first argument will be the value accumulated so far, and its second argument will be a value just provided by , TT{g}, .}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{z}, , , a new hash table, of the same class as , TT{x},  and , TT{y}, , containing the pair , TT{f(p,q) => g(t(p,q),g(b,c))},  whenever , TT{x},  contains the pair , TT{p => b},  and , TT{y},  contains the pair , TT{q => c}, , except that , TT{h},  is used to combine values when two keys coincide.  If , TT{f},  or , TT{g},  evaluates , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: continue}, , then nothing is contributed to the resulting hash table.  If , TT{h},  evaluates , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: continue}, , then, at that point, the entry stored under the key , TT{f(p,q)},  in the hash table under construction is removed.}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, The function , TT{f},  is applied to every pair , TT{(p,q)},  where , TT{p},  is a key of , TT{x},  and , TT{q},  is a key of , TT{y}, .  The number of times , TT{f},  is evaluated is thus the product of the number of keys in , TT{x},  and the number of keys in , TT{y}, ., PARA{}, The function , TT{h},  should be an associative function, for otherwise the result may depend on internal details about the implementation of hash tables that affect the order in which entries are encountered.  If , TT{f}, , , TT{t},  (if present), , TT{g}, , and , TT{h},  are commutative functions as well, then the result , TT{z},  is a commutative function of , TT{x},  and , TT{y}, ., PARA{}, The result is mutable if and only if , TT{x},  or , TT{y},  is., PARA{}, This function can be used for multiplying polynomials, where it can be used in code something like this:, PRE{     combine(x, y, monomialTimes, coeffTimes, coeffPlus)}, We illustrate that with a simple-minded implementation of the free ring on the English alphabet, representing words as string and polynomials as hash tables that associate coefficients to words., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : Poly = new Type of HashTable

o1 = Poly

o1 : Type, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : p = new Poly from { "" => 1, "x" => 2, "y" => 3, "cat" => 5 }

o2 = Poly{"" => 1   }
          "cat" => 5
          "x" => 2
          "y" => 3

o2 : Poly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : Poly * Poly := (p,q) -> combine(p,q,concatenate,times,plus);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : p*p

o4 = Poly{"" => 1       }
          "cat" => 10
          "catcat" => 25
          "catx" => 10
          "caty" => 15
          "x" => 4
          "xcat" => 10
          "xx" => 4
          "xy" => 6
          "y" => 6
          "ycat" => 15
          "yx" => 6
          "yy" => 9

o4 : Poly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, One may also use this function for multiplying divided powers in a similar manner:, PRE{     combine(x, y, monomialTimes, divPowCoeff, coeffTimes, coeffPlus)}, For example:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : DivPowPoly = new Type of HashTable

o5 = DivPowPoly

o5 : Type, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : divPowCoeff = (i,j) -> binomial(i+j,i)

o6 = divPowCoeff

                1 => 1

o7 : DivPowPoly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : DivPowPoly * DivPowPoly := (p,q) -> combine(p,q,plus,divPowCoeff,times,plus);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : p*p

o9 = DivPowPoly{0 => 1}
                1 => 2
                2 => 2

o9 : DivPowPoly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: merge}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: combine},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: CompiledFunction, compiled function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/combine-doc.m2:75:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{conductor,  -- the conductor of a finite ring map}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{conductor F, class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{conductor R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{F}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingMap, ring map}}, , , TEX{$R \rightarrow S$, a finite map with $R$ an affine reduced ring}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{R}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ring, ring}}, , , TEX{an affine domain.  In this case, $F : R \rightarrow S$ is the inclusion map of $R$ into the integral closure $S$}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , , TEX{of $R$ consisting of all $d \in R$ such that $dS \subset F(R)$}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Suppose that the ring map $F : R \rightarrow S$ is finite: i.e. $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.  The conductor of $F$ is defined to be $\{ g \in R \mid g S \subset F(R) \}$. One way to think about this is that the conductor is the set of universal denominators of , TT{S},  over , TT{R}, , or as the largest ideal of , TT{R},  which is also an ideal in , TT{S}, . An important case is the conductor of the map from a ring to its integral closure.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[x,y,z]/ideal(x^7-z^7-y^2*z^5);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : icFractions R

       3   2
      x   x
o2 = {--, --, x, y, z}
       2   z
      z

o2 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : F = icMap R

                                                    QQ[w   , w   , x..z]
                                                        5,0   4,0
o3 = map (--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------, R, {x, y, z})
                    2                          2     2       2     3   2            2      2   3          2    2
          (w   z - x , w   z - w   x, w   x - w   , w   x - y z - z , w   w    - x*y  - x*z , w    - w   y  - x z)
            4,0         5,0     4,0    5,0     4,0   5,0               5,0 4,0                 5,0    4,0

                                                       QQ[w   , w   , x..z]
                                                           5,0   4,0
o3 : RingMap -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- <-- R
                       2                          2     2       2     3   2            2      2   3          2    2
             (w   z - x , w   z - w   x, w   x - w   , w   x - y z - z , w   w    - x*y  - x*z , w    - w   y  - x z)
               4,0         5,0     4,0    5,0     4,0   5,0               5,0 4,0                 5,0    4,0, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : conductor F

             4     3   2 2   4    5
o4 = ideal (z , x*z , x z , x z, x )

o4 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If an affine domain (a ring finitely generated over a field) is given as input, then the conductor of $R$ in its integral closure is returned.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : conductor R

o5 = ideal (z , x*z , x z , x z, x )

o5 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{}, PARA{TEX{If the map is not , TT{icFractions(R)}, , then }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: pushForward}, TEX{ is called to compute the conductor.}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Caveat}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Currently this function only works if , TT{F},  comes from a integral closure computation, or is homogeneous}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{IntegralClosure :: integralClosure}}, LI{TOH{IntegralClosure :: icFractions}}, LI{TOH{IntegralClosure :: icMap}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: pushForward}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{conductor}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{conductor(Ring)}}, LI{KBD{conductor(RingMap)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{IntegralClosure :: conductor},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{IntegralClosure.m2:1942:0}, .}}}}

Cone.description:
DIV{HEADER1{Cone,  -- the class of all rational convex polyhedral cones}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A Cone represents a rational convex polyhedral cone. It need not be full dimensional or may contain a proper linear subspace. It can be zero dimensional, i.e. the origin. It is saved as a hash table which contains the generating rays and the basis of the lineality space of the cone as well as the defining half-spaces and hyperplanes. The output of a Cone looks like this:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : coneFromVData matrix {{0,0,-1,-1,1},{2,-2,1,-1,0},{1,1,1,1,0}}

o1 = Cone{...1...}

o1 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, This table displays a short summary of the properties of the Cone. The number of rays is modulo the lineality space. However, one can not access the above information directly, because this is just a virtual hash table generated for the output. The data describing a Cone is extracted by the functions included in this package. A Cone can be constructed as the positive hull (, TO{Polyhedra :: coneFromVData}, )of a set of rays or as the intersection (, TO{Polyhedra :: coneFromHData}, ) of a set of linear half-spaces and linear hyperplanes., PARA{}, As examples for the positive hull consider the following cones:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : R = matrix{{1,2,3,1},{2,3,1,1},{3,1,2,1}}

o2 = | 1 2 3 1 |
     | 2 3 1 1 |
     | 3 1 2 1 |

              3       4
o2 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : C = coneFromVData R

o3 = C

o3 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : rays C

o4 = | 2 3 1 |
     | 3 1 2 |
     | 1 2 3 |

              3       3
o4 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : LS = matrix{{1},{1},{-2}}

o5 = | 1  |
     | 1  |
     | -2 |

              3       1
o5 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : C = coneFromVData(R,LS)

o6 = C

o6 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : rays C

o7 = | 0  0 |
     | -1 1 |
     | 4  5 |

              3       2
o7 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, On the other hand, we can use these matrices as defining half-spaces and hyperplanes for the intersection:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : HS = transpose R

o8 = | 1 2 3 |
     | 2 3 1 |
     | 3 1 2 |
     | 1 1 1 |

              4       3
o8 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : C = coneFromHData HS

o9 = C

o9 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : rays C

o10 = | 1  7  -5 |
      | 7  -5 1  |
      | -5 1  7  |

               3       3
o10 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : hyperplanesTmp = transpose LS

o11 = | 1 1 -2 |

               1       3
o11 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : C = coneFromHData(HS,hyperplanesTmp)

o12 = C

o12 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : rays C

o13 = | 7  -2 |
      | -5 4  |

DIV{HEADER1{coneFromVData,  -- computes the positive hull of rays, cones, and the cone over a polyhedron}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{C = coneFromVData M , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{C = coneFromVData(M,N) , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{C = coneFromVData(C1,C2) , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{C = coneFromVData P , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{C = coneFromVData L, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{M}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , , with entries in , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{N}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , , with entries in , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{C1}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Cone, convex rational cone}}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{C2}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Cone, convex rational cone}}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{P}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron, convex polyhedron}}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{L}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{C}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Cone, convex rational cone}}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{}, Please see , TO{Polyhedra :: V- and H-representation},  on the conventions we use for cones and polyhedra., PARA{}, TT{coneFromVData},  computes the positive hull of the input. In the first two cases it considers the columns of , TT{M},  as a set of rays and the columns of , TT{N},  (if given) as generators of the lineality space and computes the cone that is the positive hull of the rays plus the lineality space. The two matrices must have the same number of rows, i.e. the columns must lie in the same ambient space. If , TT{N},  is not given or equal to 0 then the resulting cone is pointed. The rays need not be a minimal generating set of the cone. If two cones are inserted it computes their positive hull if they lie in the same ambient space. In the case of a polyhedron it computes the cone given by all positive multiples of points of the polyhedron. If applied to a list, it may contain a combination of the following in any order., UL{LI{Rays, given by a matrix , TT{R},  over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}, LI{Rays and a lineality space, given by a sequence , TT{(R,LS)},  of two matrices over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}, LI{TO{Polyhedra :: Cone}}, LI{TO{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron}}}, PARA{}, Then , TT{coneFromVData},  computes the positive hull of all inserted objects, if they are in the same ambient space, i.e. all matrices must have the same number of rows, which must equal the ambient dimension of all cones and polyhedra., PARA{}, As a first example consider the following 2 dimensional cone in 3 space:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = matrix {{1,2},{2,1},{0,0}}

o1 = | 1 2 |
     | 2 1 |
     | 0 0 |

              3       2
o1 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : C = coneFromVData R

o2 = C

o2 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, We can construct a full dimensional cone out of this one by adding a lineality space for example:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : LS = matrix {{0},{0},{1}}

o3 = | 0 |
     | 0 |
     | 1 |

              3       1
o3 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : C1 = coneFromVData (R,LS)

o4 = C1

o4 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, The resulting cone is not pointed anymore, because it contains the subspace spanned by (0,0,1). To get a full dimensional pointed cone we have to add another ray to C. For this we can apply , TT{coneFromVData},  to a list containing , TT{C},  and the new ray:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : r = matrix {{0},{1},{2}}

o5 = | 0 |
     | 1 |
     | 2 |

              3       1
o5 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : C2 = coneFromVData {C,r}

o6 = C2

o6 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, Another way would be, if we would have , TT{r},  not as a ray but already as a cone:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : r = coneFromVData r

o7 = r

o7 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, In this case we can just take the positive hull of the two cones:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : C3 = coneFromVData(C,r)

o8 = C3

o8 : Cone, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : C3 == C2

o9 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{coneFromVData}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{coneFromVData(Cone,Cone)}}, LI{KBD{coneFromVData(List)}}, LI{KBD{coneFromVData(Matrix)}}, LI{KBD{coneFromVData(Matrix,Matrix)}}, LI{KBD{coneFromVData(Polyhedron)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Polyhedra :: coneFromVData},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Polyhedra/documentation/old_documentation.m2:518:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{convexHull,  -- computing the convex hull of points, rays and polyhedra}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{P = convexHull M , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{P = convexHull(M,N) , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{P = convexHull(P1,P2) , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{P = convexHull L , class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{P = convexHull(M,N,W), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{M}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , , with entries in , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{N}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , , with entries in , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{W}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , , with entries in , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{P1}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron, convex polyhedron}}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{P2}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron, convex polyhedron}}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{L}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{P}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron, convex polyhedron}}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{}, Please see , TO{Polyhedra :: V- and H-representation},  on the conventions we use for cones and polyhedra., PARA{}, TT{convexHull},  computes the convex hull of the input. In the first two cases it considers the columns of , TT{M},  as a set of points and the columns of , TT{N},  (if given) as a set of rays and computes the polyhedron that is the convex hull of the points plus the rays. The two matrices must have the same number of rows, i.e. the columns must lie in the same ambient space. If , TT{N},  is not given or equal to 0, then the resulting polyhedron is compact and hence a polytope. The points need not be the vertices of the polyhedron. In the third case it computes the convex hull of , TT{P1},  and , TT{P2},  if they lie in the same ambient space. Finally, it computes the convex hull of a list , TT{L},  where the list may contain a combination of the following in any order., UL{LI{Points, given by a matrix , TT{M},  over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}, LI{Points and ray generators, given by a sequence , TT{(V,R)}, of two matrices over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}, LI{Points, ray generators and lineality generators, given by a sequence , TT{(M,N,W)}, of three matrices over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}}, LI{TO{Polyhedra :: Cone}}, LI{TO{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron}}}, PARA{}, Then , TT{convexHull},  computes the convex hull of all inserted objects, if they are in the same ambient space, i.e. all matrices must have the same number of rows, which must equal the ambient dimension of all cones and polyhedra., PARA{}, For example, consider the square in , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: QQ}, ^2:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : M = matrix {{1,1,-1,-1},{1,-1,1,-1}}

o1 = | 1 1  -1 -1 |
     | 1 -1 1  -1 |

              2       4
o1 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : P = convexHull M

o2 = P

o2 : Polyhedron, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, If we add a ray, then it is not compact anymore:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : r = matrix {{1},{2}}

o3 = | 1 |
     | 2 |

              2       1
o3 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : P =convexHull(M,r)

o4 = P

o4 : Polyhedron, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, If we add some more vertices to , TT{M},  then we get a hexagon:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : N = matrix {{-2,-2,0},{0,-2,-2}}

o5 = | -2 -2 0  |
     | 0  -2 -2 |

              2       3
o5 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : Q = convexHull(M|N)

o6 = Q

o6 : Polyhedron, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, Again if we add the ray , TT{r},  then the polyhedron is not compact:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : Q1 = convexHull(M|N,r)

o7 = Q1

o7 : Polyhedron, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}, To get this polyhedron we could also have used the application of , TT{convexHull},  to lists or pairs of polyhedra:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : P1 = convexHull {P,N}

o8 = P1

o9 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : P1 = convexHull(P,Q)

o10 = P1

o10 : Polyhedron, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : P1 == Q1

o11 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{convexHull}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{convexHull(List)}}, LI{KBD{convexHull(Matrix)}}, LI{KBD{convexHull(Matrix,Matrix)}}, LI{KBD{convexHull(Matrix,Matrix,Matrix)}}, LI{KBD{convexHull(Polyhedron,Polyhedron)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Polyhedra :: convexHull},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Polyhedra/documentation/old_documentation.m2:431:0}, .}}}}

ConwayPolynomials.description:
DIV{HEADER1{ConwayPolynomials,  -- database of Conway polynomials for use with GF}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{EM{ConwayPolynomials},  is a package that provides a database of Conway polynomials. A Conway polynomial for a prime p and an exponent n is a particular monic polynomial whose roots are primitive elements of a finite field with p^n elements.  They can take a very long time to compute, so the package comes with just a publicly available database of Conway polynomials provided by Frank Luebeck.}, PARA{After the package is loaded, the function , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GF},  will return Galois fields presented by Conway polynomials, provided they are in the table.  Moreover, , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: map},  can be used to produce the canonical maps between Conway Galois fields.}, PARA{The package is loaded by default when Macaulay2 starts up.  The database is loaded the first time , TO{ConwayPolynomials :: conwayPolynomial},  is called, resulting in a brief pause.}, PARA{In this example, we show how , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GF},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: map},  behave when the package is present.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : GF 125

If x is a hash table, the copy is mutable if and only if x is., PARA{}, It is not advisable to copy such things as modules and rings, for: (1) the operations that have already been installed for them will return values in the original object, rather than in the copy; and (2) the copy operation is shallow, not copying keys and values that happen to be hash tables., PARA{}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: newClass}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: copy},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: CompiledFunction, compiled function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_hashtables.m2:340:0}, .}}}}

Down.description:
DIV{HEADER1{Down,  -- monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{MonomialOrder},  -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic)., PARA{}, In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations., PARA{}, In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of , EM{ordering tests}, , of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}, ., PARA{}, Permissible elements:, UL{LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GRevLex},  => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Lex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  => {...}}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Position},  => Up  or  Position => Down}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupRevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MonomialSize},  => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variables}}, PARA{}, Some examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list., UL{LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}},  -- a product order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {2, 3}},  -- same}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}},  -- a weight order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}},  -- same}}, If any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option , TT{Global => false},  should be used., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]

o1 = QQ[x..y]

o1 : PolynomialRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : x<1

o2 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : y<1

o3 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}}, LI{TOH{QthPower :: weightGrevlex}}, LI{TOH{QthPower :: grevlexWeight}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Down},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Symbol, symbol}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_monomial_orderings.m2:704:0}, .}}}}

ehrhart.description:
DIV{HEADER1{ehrhart,  -- calculates the Ehrhart polynomial of a polytope}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{f = ehrhart P, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{P}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Polyhedra :: Polyhedron, convex polyhedron}}, , , which must be compact}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{f}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingElement, ring element}}, , , Ehrhart polynomial as element of QQ[x]}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{}, TT{ehrhart},  can only be applied to polytopes, i.e. compact polyhedra. To calculate the Ehrhart polynomial, the number of lattice points in the first n dilations of the polytope are calculated, where n is the dimension of the polytope. A system of linear equations is then solved to find the polynomial., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : P = convexHull transpose matrix {{0,0,0},{1,0,0},{0,1,0},{1,1,3}}

o1 = P

     1 3    2   3
o2 = -x  + x  + -x + 1
     2          2

o2 : QQ[x], class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{ehrhart}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{ehrhart(Polyhedron)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Polyhedra :: ehrhart},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Polyhedra/documentation/old_documentation.m2:2935:0}, .}}}}

eigenvectors.description:
DIV{HEADER1{eigenvectors,  -- find eigenvectors of a matrix over real or complex numbers}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{(eigvals, eigvecs) = eigenvectors M, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{M}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , , or a , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MutableMatrix},  over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RR},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: CC}, , which is a square n by n matrix}}}}, LI{TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: using functions with optional inputs, Optional inputs}, :, UL{LI{SPAN{TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: eigenvectors(...,Hermitian=>...), Hermitian}, TT{ => }, TT{...}, , , SPAN{default value , false}, , , SPAN{whether to assume the matrix is symmetric or Hermitian}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{eigvals}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: VerticalList, vertical list}}, , ,  a list of the eigenvalues of , TT{M}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{eigvecs}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Matrix, matrix}}, , ,  or , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MutableMatrix, mutable matrix}}, , if , TT{M},  is one), whose columns are the corresponding eigenvectors of , TT{M}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, The resulting matrix is over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: CC}, , and contains the eigenvectors of , TT{M}, .  The LAPACK and Eigen libraries are used to compute eigenvectors of real and complex matrices., PARA{}, Recall that if , TT{v},  is a non-zero vector such that , TT{Mv = av}, , for a scalar a, then , TT{v},  is called an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue , TT{a}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : M = matrix{{1, 2}, {5, 7}}

o1 = | 1 2 |
     | 5 7 |

              2       2
o1 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : eigenvectors M

o2 = ({-.358899}, | -.827138 -.262266 |)
      {8.3589  }  | .561999  -.964996 |

o2 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, If the matrix is symmetric (over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RR}, ) or Hermitian (over , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: CC}, ), this information should be provided as an optional argument , TT{Hermitian=>true}, .  In this case, the resulting eigenvalues will be returned as real numbers, and if , TT{M},  is real, the matrix of eigenvectors will be real., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : M = matrix {{1, 2}, {2, 1}}

     | 2 1 |

              2       2
o3 : Matrix ZZ  <-- ZZ, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : (e,v) = eigenvectors(M, Hermitian=>true)

o4 = ({-1}, | -.707107 .707107 |)
      {3 }  | .707107  .707107 |

o4 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : class \ e

o5 = {RR}
     {RR}

o5 : VerticalList, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : v

o6 = | -.707107 .707107 |
     | .707107  .707107 |

                2         2
o6 : Matrix RR    <-- RR
              53        53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Caveat}, The eigenvectors are approximate.}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: eigenvalues}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: SVD}}}}, MENU{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: eigenvectors(...,Hermitian=>...)}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{eigenvectors}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{eigenvectors(Matrix)}}, LI{KBD{eigenvectors(MutableMatrix)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: eigenvectors},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunctionWithOptions, method function with options}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/eigenvectors-doc.m2:42:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{eliminate, }, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{eliminate(v,J), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{v}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingElement, ring element}},  or , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}, , a variable or list of variables of a polynomial ring , TT{R}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{J}, , , SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , , in the ring , TT{R}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , , generated by the elements of J not involving the variables v}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, If the ideal , TT{J},  is homogeneous, then an effort is made to use the Hilbert function to speed up the computation., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = ZZ/101[x,a,b,c,d]	  

o1 = R

o1 : PolynomialRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : f = x^2+a*x+b

      2
o2 = x  + x*a + b

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : g = x^2+c*x+d

      2
o3 = x  + x*c + d

o3 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : time eliminate(x,ideal(f,g))

o4 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : time ideal resultant(f,g,x)
 -- used 0.00105034s (cpu); 0.00105232s (thread); 0s (gc)

                        2    2             2           2

o5 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : sylvesterMatrix(f,g,x)

o6 = {-3} | 1 a b 0 |

expectedReesIdeal.description:
DIV{HEADER1{expectedReesIdeal,  -- symmetric algebra ideal plus jacobian dual}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{J = expectedReesIdeal M, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{M}, , , SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , }}, LI{SPAN{TT{M}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Module, module}}, , }}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{J}, , , SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , }}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Let M be an R-module with g generators and free presentation phi: R^h \to R^g. The symmetric algebra of M can be written as R[T_1,\dots,T_g]/J, where J is the ideal generated by the entries of the 1 x h matrix T*m, where T = (T_1..T_g). If the entries of m are all contained in an ideal (X_1..X_n) (for example, when m is a minimal presentation and the X_i generate the maximal ideal, there is a matrix psi: R[Z]^h \to R[Z]^n such that T*phi = X*psi. Under reasonable hypotheses (eg when R is a domain) the relation X*psi = 0 in the Rees algebra implies that the n x n minors of psi are 0. Thus these minors lie in the ideal defining the Rees algebra. The expectedReesIdeal is the sum of the ideals (T*phi) and the ideal of nxn minors of psi. Under particularly good circumstances this sum is known to be equal to the ideal of the Rees algebra. More generally, it may speed computations of }, TO{ReesAlgebra :: reesIdeal}, TEX{ to start with this sum rather than with the ideal T*phi, as in the following example. (This can be turned off with the Jacobian=>false option.)}}, PARA{TEX{The term 'Expected Rees Ideal' for the sum of of the ideal of the symmetric algebra of I with the ideal of maximal minors of the Jacobian dual matrix of a presentation of I is derived from the paper "Rees Algebras of Ideals of Low Codimension", Proc. Am. Math. Soc. 1996 of Colley and Ulrich. Building on the paper "Ideals with Expected Reduction Number", Am. J. Math 1996, they prove that this ideal is in fact equal to the ideal of the Rees algebra of I when I is a codimension 2 perfect ideal whose Hilbert-Burch matrix has a special form. See }, TO{ReesAlgebra :: jacobianDual}, TEX{ for an example.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : setRandomSeed 0

Expression.description:
DIV{HEADER1{Expression,  -- the class of all expressions}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, An , EM{expression},  is a symbolic representation of a mathematical expression.  It retains some of the semantics of the mathematical expression, as well as enough information to print the expression nicely.  In Macaulay2 expressions have two main functions: they are an intermediate phase in the conversion of a mathematical object to a , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: net},  that can be printed; and they are a way of holding and displaying a mathematical expression in an unevaluated form that can be both printed and evaluated., PARA{}, Internally, each expression is a basic list whose elements may also be expressions.  The elements that are not expressions are interpreted as themselves, and may be strings, symbols, numbers, etc.  There are several types of expression that correspond to various sorts of mathematical entities, such as sums of class , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Sum}, , products, of class , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Product}, , fractions of class , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Divide}, , etc., PARA{}, Expressions are produced with the function , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: expression}, .  The various methods installed for it try to bring as much of the semantic structure of the mathematical object to light.  The following examples illustrate that, using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: peek},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: peek'},  to display the internal structure., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : expression 4

o1 = 4

o1 : Expression of class Holder, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : peek oo

o2 = Holder{4}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : d = expression (-4)

o3 = -4

o3 : Expression of class Minus, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : peek oo

o4 = Minus{4}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : QQ[x];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : f = (x+1)^5

      5     4      3      2
o6 = x  + 5x  + 10x  + 10x  + 5x + 1

o6 : QQ[x], class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : peek f

o7 = QQ[x]{x5+5x4+10x3+10x2+5x+1}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : e = expression f

      5     4      3      2
o8 = x  + 5x  + 10x  + 10x  + 5x + 1

o8 : Expression of class Sum, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : peek e

          5    4     3     2
o9 = Sum{x , 5x , 10x , 10x , 5x, 1}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : peek'_2 e

                                   4                3                2
o10 = Sum{Power{x, 5}, Product{5, x }, Product{10, x }, Product{10, x },
      -----------------------------------------------------------------------
      Product{5, x}, OneExpression{1}}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : peek'_11 e

o11 = Sum{Power{x, 5}, Product{5, Power{x, 4}}, Product{10, Power{x, 3}},
      -----------------------------------------------------------------------
      Product{10, Power{x, 2}}, Product{5, x}, OneExpression{1}}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The function , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: factor},  returns an expression., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : c = factor f

             5
o12 = (x + 1)

o12 : Expression of class Product, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : peek'_2 c

o13 = Product{Power{x + 1, 5}}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i14 : factor 240012

       2 2
o14 = 2 3 59*113

o14 : Expression of class Product, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Expressions can be evaluated using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: value}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i15 : value e

       5     4      3      2
o15 = x  + 5x  + 10x  + 10x  + 5x + 1

o15 : QQ[x], class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i16 : value e == f

o16 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i17 : value c

       5     4      3      2
o17 = x  + 5x  + 10x  + 10x  + 5x + 1

o17 : QQ[x], class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The following operators can be applied to expressions: , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: SPACE}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: *}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: **}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: +}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: -}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: /}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ==}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ^}, , and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: _}, .  They are contagious, in the sense that when applied to an expression and a non-expression, the non-expression will be converted to an expression and the operator will be applied.  Only the most trivial algebraic simplifications are applied., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i18 : d + e

             5     4      3      2
o18 = - 4 + x  + 5x  + 10x  + 10x  + 5x + 1

o18 : Expression of class Sum, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i19 : d + 4

o19 = - 4 + 4

o19 : Expression of class Sum, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i20 : d / 4

      -4
o20 = --
       4

o20 : Expression of class Divide, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i21 : d / 1

o21 = -4

o21 : Expression of class Minus, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i22 : d == e

             5     4      3      2
o22 = -4 == x  + 5x  + 10x  + 10x  + 5x + 1

o22 : Expression of class Equation, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, MENU{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: value(Expression)}, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: hold}, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Table}, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Holder}, FractionField.description: DIV{HEADER1{FractionField,  -- the class of all fraction fields}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, Macaulay2 provides for fraction fields of integral domains., PARA{}, In some cases, normal forms of fractions makes sense, but in general for fraction fieldss of quotient rings, there is no notion of normal form for a fraction. In other words, fractions may be equal without displaying the same numerator and denominator., PARA{}, Computations over fraction fields, or polynomial rings over fraction fields, especially Gröbner basis computations, are much slower than over prime fields. Still, an attempt is made to speed up these computations as much as possible, and more is planned in the future., PARA{}, For an overview, see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: fraction fields},  and  , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: frac}, ., HEADER4{Useful functions for use with fractions and fraction fields include:}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: frac}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: numerator}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: denominator}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: liftable}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: lift}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Functions and methods returning , a fraction field, :}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: frac}}}, HEADER2{Methods that use , a fraction field, :}, UL{LI{SPAN{KBD{degrees(FractionField)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: degrees(Ring)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{describe(FractionField)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: describe}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{dim(FractionField)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: dim(Ring)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{frac(FractionField)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: frac}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{numgens(FractionField)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: numgens(Ring)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{precision(FractionField)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: FractionField},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Type, type}}, , with ancestor classes , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: EngineRing},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Ring},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Type},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MutableHashTable},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: HashTable},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Thing}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/doc_rings.m2:220:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{Global,  -- monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{MonomialOrder},  -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic)., PARA{}, In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations., PARA{}, In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of , EM{ordering tests}, , of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}, ., PARA{}, Permissible elements:, UL{LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GRevLex},  => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Lex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  => {...}}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Position},  => Up  or  Position => Down}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupRevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MonomialSize},  => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variables}}, PARA{}, Some examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list., UL{LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}},  -- a product order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {2, 3}},  -- same}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}},  -- a weight order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}},  -- same}}, If any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option , TT{Global => false},  should be used., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]

o1 = QQ[x..y]

o2 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : y<1

o3 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}}, LI{TOH{QthPower :: weightGrevlex}}, LI{TOH{QthPower :: grevlexWeight}}}}, DIV{DIV{HEADER2{Functions with optional argument named , TT{Global}, :}, UL{LI{SPAN{KBD{monoid(...,Global=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: monoid(...,Local=>...)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{newRing(...,Global=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: newRing}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{symmetricAlgebra(...,Global=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: symmetricAlgebra}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{tensor(Monoid,Monoid,Global=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: tensor(Monoid,Monoid)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{tensor(Ring,Ring,Global=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: tensor(Monoid,Monoid)}}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Global},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Symbol, symbol}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_monomial_orderings.m2:704:0}, .}}}}

GRevLex.description:
DIV{HEADER1{GRevLex,  -- graded reverse lexicographical monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TEX{ The graded reverse lexicographic order is defined by: $x^A > x^B$ if either $degree(x^A) > degree(x^B)$ or $degree(x^A) = degree(x^B)$ and the LAST non-zero entry of the vector of integers $A-B$ is NEGATIVE. }, PARA{}, TEX{ This is the default order in Macaulay2, in large part because it is often the most efficient order for use with Gröbner bases.  By giving GRevLex a list of integers, one may change the definition of the order: $degree(x^A)$ is the dot product of $A$ with the argument of GRevLex.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[a..d];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : a^3 + b^2 + b*c

      3    2
o2 = a  + b  + b*c

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : S = QQ[a..d, MonomialOrder => GRevLex => {1,2,3,4}];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : a^3 + b^2 + b*c

            2    3
o4 = b*c + b  + a

o4 : S, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The largest possible exponent of variables in the , TT{GRevLex},  order is 2^31-1.  For efficiency reasons, it is sometimes useful to limit the size of monomials (this often makes computations more efficient)., Use , TT{MonomialSize => 16}, , which allows maximal exponent 2^15-1, or , TT{MonomialSize => 8}, , which allows maximal exponent 2^7-1., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : B1 = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16,MonomialOrder=>GRevLex];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : B = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : a^(2^15-1)

      32767
o7 = a

o7 : B, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : C = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>8,MonomialOrder=>GRevLex];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : try a^(2^15-1) else "failed"

o9 = failed, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : a^(2^7-1)

       127
o10 = a

hilbertPolynomial.description: DIV{HEADER1{hilbertPolynomial,  -- compute the Hilbert polynomial}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, In a singly graded ambient ring, the , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: hilbertFunction, Hilbert function},  eventually is a polynomial called the Hilbert polynomial. By default this polynomial is written in terms of the Hilbert polynomials of projective spaces because it is a good form for extracting geometric information from the polynomial. A good choice of , TT{D},  may speed up the calculations?}}, LI{SPAN{TO2{IntegralClosure :: icFracP(...,Limit=>...), Limit}, TT{ => }, TT{...}, , , SPAN{default value , infinity}, , , if value N is given, perform N loop steps only}}, LI{SPAN{TO2{IntegralClosure :: icFracP(...,Verbosity=>...), Verbosity}, TT{ => }, TT{...}, , , SPAN{default value , 0}, , , if value is greater than 0, report the conductor element and number of steps in the loop}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{The module generators of the integral closure of , TT{R},  in its total ring of fractions.  The generators are given as elements in the total ring of fractions.}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, Input is an equidimensional reduced ring in characteristic p that is finitely and separably generated over the base field. The output is a finite set of fractions that generate the integral closure as an , TT{R}, -module. An intermediate step in the code is the computation of a conductor element , TT{D},  that is a non-zerodivisor; its existence is guaranteed by the separability assumption. The user may supply , TT{D},  with the optional , TT{ConductorElement => D}, . (Sometimes, but not always, supplying , TT{D},  speeds up the computation.) In any case, with the non-zero divisor , TT{D}, , the algorithm starts by setting the initial approximation of the integral closure to be the finitely generated , TT{R}, -module , TT{(1/D)R}, , and in the subsequent loop the code recursively constructs submodules. Eventually two submodules repeat; the repeated module is the integral closure of , TT{R}, . The user may optionally provide , TT{Limit => N},  to stop the loop after , TT{N},  steps, and the optional , TT{Verbosity => 1},  reports the conductor element and the number of steps it took for the loop to stabilize. The algorithm is based on the Leonard--Pellikaan--Singh--Swanson algorithm., PARA{}, A simple example., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = ZZ/5[x,y,z]/ideal(x^6-z^6-y^2*z^4);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : icFracP R

ImmutableType.description:
DIV{HEADER1{ImmutableType,  -- the class of all immutable types}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, All types are implemented as hash tables.  Most types are mutable, so that additional methods for handling their instances can be added at any time.  However, if a type has an ancestor where the methods can be stored, then mutability is not needed., PARA{}, When a type is used to represent a mathematical object, then immutability is desirable, in order to make the strict equality operator work on it.  For example, a module , TT{M},  is a type, with its elements are its instances, but we would like to be able to compare two modules quickly, and form sets of modules.  This is possible, because we have implemented modules as immutable types, and we have put the methods for adding and subtracting elements of , TT{M},  into the class , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Vector}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : F = ZZ^3

       3

o3 = 4, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : A = ZZ[a..d]; B = A[r,s,t]; C = B[x,y,z]

o7 = 0, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : index z

o8 = 2, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : index r

o9 = 0, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Notice that r is an element of B, and so indices are taken from that ring. If we consider r as an element of C, we get a different answer. DIV{HEADER1{IntegralClosure,  -- routines for integral closure of affine domains and ideals}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{This package contains several algorithms for computing the integral closure (i.e. normalization) of an affine domain, and also of an ideal.}}, PARA{TEX{The basic use of this package is shown in the following example.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[x,y,z]/(x^3-x^2*z^5-z^2*y^5)

o1 = R

o1 : QuotientRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : S = integralClosure R

o2 = S

o2 : QuotientRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : describe S

                         QQ[w   , x..z]
                             1,0
o3 = -----------------------------------------------------
               3        2       5    2   2        5

       1,0          1,0                  1,0, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Use }, TO{IntegralClosure :: icFractions}, TEX{ to see what fractions have been added.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : icFractions R

       3
      y z
o4 = {---, x, y, z}
       x

       1,0

o6 : Ideal of QQ[w   , x..z]
                  1,0, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The integral closure of an ideal can be computed as follows.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : use R
